summary: Removes a restriction on the MPLS reserved labels IPv4 Explicit NULL and IPv6 Explicit NULL. They were previously legal only at the bottom of the label stack; this document allows them anywhere in the stack. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS packets carry a stack of labels. Two label values are reserved as a way of saying that the stack should end there. The original rules allowed them only in one place, the bottom of the stack, and said nothing about what to do otherwise. This document removes that restriction, so the two label values may now appear anywhere, and it says exactly what a router should do when it pops one of them.

subtitle: A rule change that lets two reserved MPLS labels appear anywhere in a label stack, not only at the bottom.

tldr.problem: RFC 3032 said the reserved IPv4 and IPv6 Explicit NULL labels were only legal at the bottom of an MPLS label stack, without giving a reason, and no MPLS specification said what a receiver should do with a packet that broke the rule.
tldr.mechanism: The document rewrites the two paragraphs of RFC 3032 that carried the restriction, so that popping an Explicit NULL label now always means the stack is popped and the label beneath, if any, takes over the forwarding decision.
tldr.outcome: This makes the Pipe Model for Differentiated Services work over MPLS, where the egress has to put Explicit NULL on top of a label stack that still carries the tunnelled packet.

today: RFC 4182 is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by RFC 5462 and RFC 7274. It remains the document that lifted the restriction on where the Explicit NULL labels may appear in an MPLS label stack.

sections.title: The Restriction Being Removed
sections.content:
RFC 3032 defines a reserved label value known as IPv4 Explicit NULL and a reserved label value known as IPv6 Explicit NULL. It states that these label values are only legal at the bottom of the MPLS label stack. However, no reason is given for this restriction.

It has turned out that in practice there are some situations in which it is useful to send MPLS packets that have Explicit NULL occur somewhere other than at that bottom of the label stack. While the intended semantics are obvious enough, the fact that such packets are gratuitously declared by RFC 3032 to be illegal has made it difficult to handle these situations in an interoperable manner.

This document updates RFC 3032 by removing the unnecessary restriction, so that the two label values are legal anywhere in the label stack.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule existed but nobody could say why. In practice, engineers kept running into packets that broke it, and because the standards did not say what a router should do with such a packet, two implementations could behave differently and the network would not work.

sections.title: The New Wording for RFC 3032
sections.content:
RFC 3032 stated that a value of 0 represents the IPv4 Explicit NULL Label and that this label value is only legal at the bottom of the label stack, and that a value of 2 represents the IPv6 Explicit NULL Label with the same restriction. This document changes both paragraphs.

Paragraph i now reads that a value of 0 represents the IPv4 Explicit NULL Label, that an IPv4 Explicit NULL at the top of the label stack means that the stack must be popped, and that if the NULL was not the only label on the stack, this will cause the label beneath it to rise to the top of the stack, with the disposition of the packet based on the label that has now risen to the top. If, on the other hand, the NULL was the only label on the stack, then the stack is now empty, and the resulting packet is treated as an IPv4 packet with its disposition based on the IPv4 header.

Paragraph iii says the same for the IPv6 Explicit NULL Label, except that an empty stack leaves a packet treated as an IPv6 packet, with its disposition based on the IPv6 header.
sections.plainLanguage: The new text is deliberately short. A router that finds an Explicit NULL label pops the stack. If there are labels left underneath, the next one up takes over the job of deciding where the packet goes. If the stack is now empty, the packet is just an ordinary IP packet again.

sections.title: Why the Restriction Caused Trouble
sections.content:
Restricting Explicit NULL to the bottom of the stack has caused some problems in practice. With the restriction in place, one should not distribute, to a particular label distribution peer, a binding of Explicit NULL to a particular Forwarding Equivalence Class unless the following condition, called Condition L, holds: all MPLS packets received by that peer with an incoming label corresponding to that FEC contain only a single label stack entry. If Explicit NULL is bound to the FEC but Condition L does not hold, the peer is being requested to create illegal packets. None of the MPLS specifications say what the peer is actually supposed to do in this case. The situation is made more troublesome by the facts that, in practice, Condition L rarely holds, and that it is not possible in general to determine whether it holds or not.

Some implementations simply transmit the illegal packet. Others try to convert it to a legal packet by stripping off the Explicit NULL before transmitting it, which breaks the Pipe Model by discarding the LSP Diff-Serv information. It is conceivable that there may be an implementation that drops the illegal packet entirely, which would also break the Pipe Model, as it would lose not only the LSP Diff-Serv information but the entire packet.
sections.plainLanguage: A router could be told to use the Explicit NULL label for a certain kind of traffic, and then find itself sending packets that the rules said were illegal. There was no safe answer, so implementations did different things: some sent the packet anyway, some quietly removed the label, and some threw the packet away.

sections.title: How the Pipe Model Uses Explicit NULL
sections.content:
There are good reasons to create label stacks in which Explicit NULL is at the top of the label stack but a non-null label is at the bottom, when supporting the Pipe Model of RFC 3270, which specifies the procedures for MPLS support of Differentiated Services. RFC 3270 defines a Pipe Model in which tunneled packets must convey two meaningful pieces of Diff-Serv information: the LSP Diff-Serv Information, which is meaningful to intermediate nodes along the LSP span including the LSP Egress but is not meaningful beyond the LSP Egress and is ignored there; and the Tunneled Diff-Serv Information, which is meaningful beyond the LSP Egress, is conveyed by the LSP Ingress to the LSP Egress, and is not meaningful to the intermediate nodes on the LSP span.

When the Pipe Model is in use, it is common practice for the LSP Egress to bind Explicit Null to the tunnel's FEC. The intention is that the LSP Diff-Serv information will be carried in the EXP bits of the Explicit NULL label stack entry, and the tunneled Diff-Serv information will be carried in whatever is below the Explicit NULL label stack entry, that is, in the IP header DS bits or in the EXP bits of the next entry on the MPLS label stack. Naturally this causes a problem if the Pipe Model LSP is being used to tunnel MPLS packets, that is, if Condition L does not hold, because with strict adherence to RFCs 3031 and 3036 the result is an MPLS packet where Explicit NULL is at the top of the label stack even though it is not the only entry in the stack. However, RFC 3032 makes this packet illegal.

The LSP Egress is not compelled to bind Explicit NULL to the tunnel's FEC, since an ordinary label could be used instead. However, using Explicit NULL enables the egress to determine immediately, without a lookup in the Label Information Base, that the further forwarding of the packet is to be determined by whatever is below the label. Avoiding this lookup can have favourable implications on forwarding performance. Removing the restriction that Explicit Null only occur at the bottom of the stack is the simplest way to facilitate the proper operation of the Pipe Model.
sections.plainLanguage: The Pipe Model needs two pieces of service-quality information in one packet: one that matters to the routers along the tunnel, and one that matters to whoever receives the tunnel. Explicit NULL is the natural place to put the first, with the second carried underneath it. That is only possible if Explicit NULL can sit on top of another label, which is exactly what this document allows.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations that adhere to this specification will interoperate correctly, and will correctly support the Pipe Model.

Implementations that do not adhere to this specification may not interoperate. In particular, if a router advertises a binding of Explicit NULL and that router has an upstream LDP peer that will not transmit a packet that has multiple label stack entries with Explicit NULL at the top of the stack, then it will not be possible to use Explicit NULL to support the Pipe Model until the upstream LDP peer is brought into compliance with this specification.

It is possible that there may be a router implementation, preceding this specification, that will discard any received packet with multiple label stack entries and a top label value of Explicit Null. It is advisable to configure any such routers so that they do not advertise any bindings to Explicit Null.
sections.plainLanguage: Old equipment may still refuse these packets, so the change has to be made from both ends. Until the neighbour that sends the packet is upgraded too, the safe move is not to advertise the Explicit NULL binding at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document updates RFC 3032 by allowing Explicit NULL to occur at any position in the label stack. This modification does not impose any new security considerations beyond those discussed in RFC 3032.
sections.plainLanguage: Allowing a label in more places does not change how packets are protected, so the document adds nothing new here. The security analysis stays where it was, in the document that defines the label stack.

viz.caption: THE TWO RESERVED LABELS AND WHERE THEY MAY APPEAR

items.title: Label value 0
items.text: The IPv4 Explicit NULL Label. It says to pop the stack and forward on the IPv4 header.

items.title: Label value 2
items.text: The IPv6 Explicit NULL Label. It says to pop the stack and forward on the IPv6 header.

items.title: Where it was allowed
items.text: Only at the bottom of the label stack, under the original rule in RFC 3032.

items.title: Where it is allowed now
items.text: Anywhere in the label stack, after this document.

cells: The stack is emptied and the IP header decides the disposition
The stack is popped; if other labels remain, the one beneath rises to the top

viz.caption: THE REPLACEMENT WORDING FOR THE IPv4 EXPLICIT NULL LABEL

data.title: RFC 3032 paragraph i, as changed
data.code:
i. A value of 0 represents the "IPv4 Explicit NULL Label".

   An IPv4 Explicit NULL at the top of the label stack means that
   the stack must be popped.

   If the NULL was not the only label on the stack, this will
   cause the label beneath it to rise to the top of the stack.
   The disposition of the packet is based on the label that has
   now risen to the top.

   If, on the other hand, the NULL was the only label on the
   stack, then the stack is now empty.  The resulting packet is
   treated as an IPv4 packet, and its disposition is based on the
   IPv4 header.

viz.caption: THE TWO PIECES OF INFORMATION IN A PIPE MODEL PACKET

items.title: LSP Diff-Serv information
items.text: Meaningful to the nodes along the tunnel, and carried in the EXP bits of the Explicit NULL label.

items.title: Tunneled Diff-Serv information
items.text: Meaningful beyond the tunnel egress, and carried in the IP header DS bits or the EXP bits of the next label.

items.title: Why Explicit NULL
items.text: It lets the egress decide at once that forwarding continues with whatever is below the label, with no lookup in the Label Information Base.
